title: Unit 1 Assessment — Cybersecurity
intro: Answer every question. You get your score at the end — you can't change answers after finishing.

blocks.html:
📋 Before you start

This assessment covers everything from the unit: phishing, passwords and encryption.

  • Answer every question — there are 7.
  • No hints, no retries: this is the real thing.
  • Press Finish & see my score at the end.

options: Tricking a person into giving away private details
Guessing a password by trying every combination
Blocking a website with too much traffic

blocks.prompt: An email says your account will be deleted in ONE HOUR unless you click a link. What is the safest response?
options: Click quickly before time runs out
Reply and ask if it is real
Don't click — go to the real website yourself
Forward it to friends as a warning

blocks.prompt: Put these passwords in order of strength — weakest first

blocks.text: Encryption scrambles a message so only someone with the [[key]] can read it. A Caesar cipher moves every letter along the [[alphabet]] by the same amount, which is called the [[shift|key]].

blocks.prompt: Why does two-factor authentication make an account safer?
options: A hacker needs your password AND your phone
It hides your password from the website
It stops the website being hacked

blocks.prompt: Give TWO warning signs that an email might be phishing.
blocks.model: pressure to act fast, and a suspicious sender address, link, or request for details
keywordLabels: mentions a suspicious sender, link or request

blocks.prompt: Why is a LONG password made of random words stronger than a short one with symbols?
blocks.model: length multiplies the possible combinations, so it takes far longer to guess or crack
keywordLabels: explains more combinations / longer to crack

phishing.label: spotting phishing
phishing.strength: You can spot the tricks phishing emails use — pressure, fake senders and dodgy links don't fool you.
phishing.target: Practise spotting phishing warning signs — check who sent it and what it's really asking for before you act.

passwords.label: strong passwords
passwords.strength: You understand what genuinely makes a password strong and why accounts stay safer with it.
passwords.target: Work on what makes passwords strong — remember that length beats symbols, and reusing one is the biggest risk.

encryption.label: encryption
encryption.strength: Encryption makes sense to you — keys, ciphers and shifts hold no mystery.
encryption.target: Revise how encryption scrambles a message and what the key or shift actually does.

perfectTarget: Full marks! Stretch yourself: use the tasks below to explain the ideas as if teaching Year 7.

phishing.title: Phishing drill
phishing.note: Get both right — you'll get a hint if you slip.

questions.q: A message says you've won a prize you never entered. What is it?
questions.why: Unexpected prizes are classic bait to make you click.

questions.q: What's the best FIRST check on a suspicious email?
questions.why: Fake senders give themselves away in the address, not the logo.

phishing.text: Never click a [[link]] in an unexpected email — go to the real [[website|site]] yourself and log in there.

phishing.prompt: Write a two-sentence warning for Year 7s about phishing emails.

passwords.title: Password drill
passwords.note: Get both right — you'll get a hint if you slip.

questions.why: Every extra character multiplies the combinations to guess.

questions.q: Why is reusing one password everywhere risky?
questions.hint: What happens if just one site is hacked?
questions.why: A single leaked site hands attackers all your accounts.

passwords.text: A strong password is [[long]] above all — every extra character multiplies the [[combinations|possibilities]] a hacker must try.

passwords.prompt: Explain to a Year 7 why 'correct-horse-battery-42!' beats 'P@ss1'.

encryption.title: Encryption drill
encryption.note: Get both right — you'll get a hint if you slip.

questions.q: What does the key do in encryption?
questions.why: Without the key, the scrambled message stays unreadable.

questions.q: In a Caesar cipher with shift 3, A becomes…
questions.hint: Count three letters forward from A.
questions.why: A→B→C→D: each letter moves along by the shift.

encryption.text: In a Caesar cipher, moving letters by the [[shift|key]] scrambles the message; moving them back [[decrypts|unscrambles]] it.

encryption.prompt: Describe how you cracked the cipher in the escape lesson — what did you try first?
